## 3. Methods (how the numbers were computed)

Phoneme sequences were obtained by tokenizing the IPA column (base symbol plus length, dental and pharyngealization marks; a+j and a+w merged into diphthongs), which restores four phonemes dropped in the original sequences. For each adjacent phoneme pair, the count was the sum over words of the word's frequency (token-weighted) or of 1 (type-based) times its occurrences in the word. Surprisal of a bigram is -log2 of its count divided by the total count of bigrams with the same first phoneme. Leave-one-out versions remove a word's own contribution from the counts before computing its surprisal. A word's average surprisal is the mean over its bigrams. Frequency is on the Zipf scale. Models are OLS on standardized variables with HC3 robust standard errors; cross-validated R2 uses 5 folds (seed 0).

## 7. Limitations

- The pronunciations in the data look partly automatic (for example, some vowels appear wrong); errors flow into every surprisal value. Check a sample.
- Frequency has a floor (no word below 411 occurrences), so nothing can be said about rare words.
- A bigram model ignores morphology and anything longer than two phonemes.
- With about 30,000 words almost every coefficient is significant; interpret effect sizes and cross-validated R2.
- About 90 words share an IPA transcription with another word. Token-weighted surprisal contains the word's own frequency (see the leave-one-out versions).
